company_profile.company_stage: large public creative software, document cloud, and digital experience company

sources.title: Adobe homepage
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe publicly positions itself around creativity, documents, digital experience, content workflows, marketing technology, and AI-supported creative and business tools.

sources.title: Adobe careers page
sources.public_safe_signal: Careers messaging emphasizes creativity, customer impact, innovation, inclusion, learning, and work across product, engineering, sales, design, and operations.

sources.title: Adobe investor relations
sources.public_safe_signal: Investor materials provide public context for subscription businesses, digital media, digital experience, AI strategy, customer retention, and growth risk.

sources.title: Evolving Adobe's Values and Culture (CEO memo)
sources.public_safe_signal: A CEO memo describes four Adobe values: create the future through customer-centric innovation, own the outcome with a bias to action, raise the bar with intellectual honesty, and be genuine through inclusion and respect.

sources.title: How We Hire at Adobe
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe outlines a five-step hiring process and asks for evidence of impact and creativity, portfolio or GitHub links, measurable examples, and role-specific exercises such as coding, system design, creative briefs, or scenario discussions.

sources.title: Adobe for All
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe for All describes a culture where all employees can make an impact, great ideas can come from anywhere, pay is reviewed twice yearly, and wellbeing benefits support people personally and professionally.

sources.title: Investing in the Future of Creative Cloud Extensibility: UXP Comes to Our Flagship Applications
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's developer blog describes a multi-year platform investment to move flagship apps to a modern extensibility architecture, including security, migration planning, backward compatibility, and a phased developer ecosystem transition.

sources.title: About Adobe
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's mission is to empower everyone to create; it describes AI as amplifying human ingenuity, trained for commercial safety, paired with content authenticity standards, and embedded in existing customer workflows.

sources.title: Adobe Investor Relations
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's investor page describes a diversified software company with more than 30,000 employees and fiscal 2025 revenue of $23.77 billion, positioned around creativity, productivity, and personalized customer experiences.

sources.title: Adobe AI Overview
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's AI overview says generative AI should assist and amplify human ingenuity and commits to responsible development with respect for creator rights.

sources.title: Corporate Social Responsibility at Adobe
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's responsibility page ties Adobe for All to the belief that great ideas come from anywhere and that respected, included people are more creative; it links responsible technology to AI ethics, security, privacy, trust, accessibility, and sustainability.

sources.title: Adobe Trust Center
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's Trust Center commits to protecting the security, privacy, and availability of products, systems, and data, and points to content moderation policies, government-request transparency, and public trust reports.

sources.title: AI and Your Hiring Experience
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe asks candidates to show concrete examples of how AI amplified their impact, workflows, or thinking rather than simply listing AI skills. It says human judgment must guide AI, values authenticity and integrity, and prohibits AI recording, live scribing, or prompting tools during hiring conversations unless invited.

sources.title: Adobe Research Careers
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe Research describes a team of research scientists, engineers, artists, and designers combining academic discovery with product impact, hiring full-time research scientists, research engineers, and interns in the US, London, and Bangalore, and moving early-stage technology into Adobe products.

sources.title: Adobe Design Careers
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe Design lists disciplines including brand, product, content, visual, motion, and design engineering alongside product management, program management, research and strategy, and content strategy, and describes mentorship, internal mobility, and an annual design summit.

sources.title: Recruiting Scams
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's recruiting-scam page limits legitimate recruiting email to a defined set of Adobe domains, says Adobe never requests bank details, Social Security numbers, or similar sensitive data during recruiting or offers, never charges application or equipment fees, and keeps applications and offer letters in secure platforms.

sources.title: Adobe applicant privacy policy
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's applicant privacy policy lists the candidate data it collects and states that automated systems using machine-learning techniques may analyze application information to select and retain candidates where consent is not required.

sources.title: Career site personal information requests
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's careers site says deletion requests are reviewed and answered within 30 days, that deleting data withdraws active applications and job-alert subscriptions, and that some information may be retained as legally required.

sources.title: How Adobe continues to inspire great performance and support career growth
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's Check-in page says Adobe replaced annual performance reviews and ratings in 2012 with ongoing two-way conversations, now holds quarterly check-ins, uses documented goals and stakeholder feedback, has no formal rating or ranking, lets managers set salary and equity from performance, and offers a Career Discovery tool for internal mobility; the page does not state when this description was last updated.

sources.title: Teams at Adobe
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's teams page lists distinct career areas including Engineering and Product, Design, Research, Sales, Global Marketing, Finance and Operations, Information Technology, Customer Experience, Legal and Government Relations, and Employee Experience, each with a short description of its mission.

sources.title: Build-time Wasm module splitting for faster startup (Adobe Developers Blog)
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe engineers describe replacing profile-guided WebAssembly splitting with a build-time call-graph and debug-info analysis, trading profiling effort for repeatable builds, and they document limitations and rule maintenance costs.

sources.title: Adobe Developers Live 2026 recap: CEP to UXP migration and ecosystem roadmap
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's developer recap describes a multi-year extensibility transition, stating that legacy CEP plugins keep working through 2029 while UXP becomes the future, alongside new APIs, community tooling, and open roundtable discussion.

sources.title: University and early-career programs at Adobe
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's university page says interns and new graduates work on mission-critical products across engineering, sales, and marketing, invites non-technical candidates to bring bold ideas, drive, and a clear voice, and frames early-career growth through Sales Academy and Digital Academy programs under a raise-the-bar message.

sources.title: Adobe Sales Academy
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's Sales Academy page says the program's mission is to cultivate emerging sales talent who demonstrate Adobe's core values while contributing measurable pipeline and revenue impact, combining structured training with placement into business development roles.

sources.title: Ask Adobe Design: how applicants stand out in design interviews
sources.public_safe_signal: In an Adobe Design article, eight design managers describe what makes candidates stand out: crediting collaborators while stating one's own contribution, telling the story of why the work mattered and who it served, earning cross-functional buy-in, showing humility and self-awareness, and explaining how they handled mistakes or hard feedback.

sources.title: What a design system product manager does at Adobe
sources.public_safe_signal: An Adobe Design role profile describes a design-system product manager who sets vision and strategy with product and platform teams, gathers requirements across Express, Creative Cloud and Document Cloud, prioritises roadmap work, and uses research and adoption data to guide decisions.

sources.title: Strengthening infrastructure and supply chain security in an AI-accelerated threat landscape
sources.public_safe_signal: Adobe's security blog says AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and that patching takes time in practice, so Adobe uses AI-assisted exposure detection, virtual patching and layered mitigations during remediation windows, infrastructure inventory and ownership, dependency and open-source monitoring, contextual risk prioritization, and sandboxing or malware analysis. It states that static severity scores alone can misstate real exposure and that upstream fixes may lag.

culture_principles.name: Create the future
culture_principles.description: Adobe frames generative AI as assisting and amplifying human ingenuity, with responsible development and respect for creator rights, extending its customer-centric innovation stance.

culture_principles.name: Own the outcome
culture_principles.description: The company values a bias toward action and empowerment, measuring work by the broader outcome it drives rather than only by assigned tasks.

culture_principles.name: Raise the bar
culture_principles.description: Adobe describes continuous improvement and intellectual honesty, including direct discussion of what is not going well, as central to raising performance.

culture_principles.name: Be genuine
culture_principles.description: Being genuine is tied to inclusion, respect, honesty, and reflecting the diversity of the world in the workforce.

culture_principles.name: Creativity as a company-wide capability
culture_principles.description: Adobe for All states that great ideas can come from anywhere and that respected, included people are more creative, innovative, and successful.

culture_principles.name: Responsible technology as a product commitment
culture_principles.description: Adobe connects responsible technology to AI ethics, security, privacy, trust, accessibility, and sustainability, not only to legal compliance.

culture_principles.name: Creativity for all
culture_principles.description: Adobe describes supporting creators of all ages, backgrounds, and skill levels so they can express themselves and build careers.

culture_principles.name: Scale across diversified customer workflows
culture_principles.description: Adobe presents itself as a diversified software company serving creators, businesses, and enterprises across creativity, productivity, and personalization.

culture_principles.name: Trust as a product foundation
culture_principles.description: Adobe's Trust Center frames security, privacy, availability, content moderation, and transparency as commitments that make customer experiences trustworthy, not as back-office compliance.

culture_principles.name: Human judgment guides AI
culture_principles.description: Adobe says tools do not create and people do, so it looks for candidates who pair their own creative capacity with responsible AI use rather than substituting generated output for judgment.

culture_principles.name: Authenticity in the hiring conversation
culture_principles.description: Adobe asks candidates to lead with their own voice and says being genuine is core to the company, so AI may clarify or organize thinking but must not replace the person's experience or point of view.

culture_principles.name: Design as a cross-functional discipline
culture_principles.description: Adobe Design presents design engineering, research and strategy, content strategy, and product management as parts of one design organization, with an annual summit for the whole team.

culture_principles.name: Research with a product destination
culture_principles.description: Adobe Research pairs academic discovery with transfer into Adobe product features, framing research impact in terms of shipped capabilities rather than publications alone.

culture_principles.name: Published limits on candidate data use
culture_principles.description: Adobe discloses the categories of applicant data it collects, that machine-learning systems may analyze applications where consent is not required, and how deletion requests affect active applications and retention.

culture_principles.name: Ongoing feedback instead of annual ratings
culture_principles.description: Adobe says it replaced annual reviews and ratings with Check-in, an ongoing two-way conversation supported by quarterly check-ins, documented goals, and stakeholder feedback, with no formal rating or ranking.

culture_principles.name: Internal mobility as part of growth
culture_principles.description: Adobe describes a Career Discovery tool that shows employees where people in similar roles have moved inside the company and lets them set alerts for target roles, making internal movement a visible part of career development.

culture_principles.name: Migration stewardship over forced cutovers
culture_principles.description: Adobe's developer communications pair a UXP roadmap with a stated compatibility window for existing CEP plugins, framing ecosystem transition as a managed, multi-year commitment rather than an abrupt switch.

culture_principles.name: Measure the critical path, then redesign the build
culture_principles.description: Adobe engineers describe attacking startup performance by changing how the build identifies startup-critical code, and they publish the limits of the approach rather than presenting it as universally applicable.

culture_principles.name: Early-career ownership, not observation
culture_principles.description: Adobe's university page says interns and graduates work on mission-critical products and are expected to contribute real work rather than observe from the sidelines.

culture_principles.name: Core values measured with commercial impact
culture_principles.description: Adobe's Sales Academy states its mission as developing emerging sales talent who demonstrate Adobe's core values while contributing measurable pipeline and revenue impact.

culture_principles.name: Security as continuous operational discipline
culture_principles.description: Adobe's security writing frames resilience as ongoing work in visibility, ownership, monitoring, layered mitigation, and adaptation across infrastructure and third-party dependencies, not as a one-time patch cycle. It explicitly notes that unknown or unmaintained systems create risk and that fixes can lag.

hiring_signals.signal: Shows impact and creativity in work samples rather than listing responsibilities, including a portfolio or GitHub for creative and technical roles.
Prepares specific examples with measurable impact and asks thoughtful questions about the role's impact and team dynamics.
Demonstrates problem-solving in the format the role uses, such as coding and system design, creative briefs and design thinking, or scenario-based discussion.
Shows eagerness to learn and apply AI within the craft as tools and workflows evolve.
Connects product or craft decisions to customer workflows and business outcomes.
Shows how AI or platform work improved a real customer workflow, including quality, trust, or adoption evidence.
Explains governance or trust tradeoffs in product decisions, such as privacy, content authenticity, or responsible AI.
Shows inclusive collaboration by inviting ideas from people outside their discipline or level.
Describes concrete security, privacy, or content-moderation controls they shipped, not only the policies they endorsed.
Shows concrete examples of AI improving a real workflow, decision, or creative outcome rather than listing AI tools or skills.
Explains where human judgment overrode or corrected AI output, and why.
Keeps their own voice and specific experience visible when describing AI-assisted work.
For research roles, shows research that moved toward a product surface, and can explain the engineering and product constraints it had to satisfy.
For design roles, presents portfolio work with the candidate's specific decisions, process, and collaboration across research, content, product, or engineering.
For design engineering roles, shows both design craft and implementation, not only static mockups.
For research engineering roles, explains how they built or scaled the systems behind research prototypes.
Asks informed questions about how application data and automated analysis are used, rather than assuming either a fully manual or fully automated process.
Shows a pattern of seeking feedback regularly and changing their work before a formal review cycle, consistent with Adobe's described Check-in model.
Can explain what they want to learn next and how a move inside the company would build on their current role, rather than treating career growth as only external.

For corporate or customer-facing roles, connects their experience to a specific Adobe function such as IT, finance and operations, customer experience, legal and government relations, or employee experience.
For platform engineering roles, reasons about startup cost, bundle size, and build pipelines with measured tradeoffs rather than intuition alone.
For ecosystem or developer-facing roles, accounts for backward compatibility, deprecation timelines, and developer communication.
Describes engineering constraints and failure modes honestly, including where a chosen approach does not generalize.
For early-career roles, shows drive and a clear point of view even without a technical background.
Connects values-driven behavior to measurable commercial outcomes such as pipeline or revenue in go-to-market answers.
Uses structured training and feedback as a platform to accelerate rather than waiting for scope to be assigned.
For design roles, names collaborators and separates their own contribution from the team's when presenting work.
For design roles, tells the story of why the work mattered, who it served, and what changed, rather than walking through screens.
For design roles, describes the hardest feedback or mistake they owned and what they changed in how they work.
For design-system or platform design roles, shows prioritisation across several product teams using requirements, research, and adoption evidence.
Explains risk in terms of real exposure and compensating controls rather than severity labels alone.

anti_signals.anti_signal: A resume or portfolio that lists responsibilities without evidence of impact, creativity, or technical judgment.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe's hiring guidance explicitly asks candidates to showcase work that illustrates impact and creativity rather than duties; this is a preparation signal, not an official disqualifier.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Defending the status quo or avoiding direct discussion of what is not working.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe's stated value of raising the bar emphasizes intellectual honesty and directness about shortcomings.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Treating AI as outside one's craft rather than a capability to learn and apply.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe says it looks for candidates eager to innovate with AI; this indicates an adaptability gap and is not presented as an official hiring requirement.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Framing AI only as a way to replace human craft rather than extend it.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe publicly frames AI as assisting and amplifying human ingenuity; this is a culture-fit signal, not an official disqualifier.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Treating trust, privacy, or content provenance as someone else's problem in product work.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe ties responsible technology to AI ethics, privacy, trust, and content authenticity across its product work.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Crediting only a single creative genius for outcomes that required cross-functional adoption.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe states that great ideas come from anywhere and emphasizes inclusive, cross-functional creativity.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Treating trust, security, or content moderation as a compliance page rather than a product requirement.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe's Trust Center ties these areas to product and data protection commitments; this is a preparation signal, not an official disqualifier.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Listing AI skills or tools without evidence of how they changed the work or its impact.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe explicitly asks candidates to show how AI amplified impact rather than simply naming AI skills; this is a preparation signal, not an official disqualifier.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Using AI recording, live scribing, or prompting tools during a hiring conversation without being invited.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe's hiring guidance explicitly prohibits these uses unless the candidate is invited to use them.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Presenting AI-generated work or answers that do not reflect the candidate's own experience.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe says it wants to meet the person, not an AI-generated version, and that authenticity and integrity are part of how it evaluates contributions.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Presenting portfolio work without stating what the candidate personally decided, built, or changed.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe Design describes a collaborative, cross-disciplinary design organization, so individual contribution has to be separated from team output.

anti_signals.anti_signal: For research roles, listing publications or prototypes without explaining product relevance or constraints.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe Research frames its mission around transferring early-stage technology into product features.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Replying to a recruiting message from a domain outside Adobe's published recruiting domains.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe lists the only email domains its recruiting communications can come from and warns that other contacts may be fraudulent.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Providing bank account, Social Security, or similar sensitive personal data during an Adobe interview or offer process.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe says it does not request that information during recruiting, interviews, or offers, and that its process runs through secure platforms.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Paying an application or equipment fee to secure an Adobe role.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe says it never requests money to participate in its hiring process.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Treating an offer as verified without confirming it came through Adobe's secure application or offer platform.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe says its application process and offer letters are managed through secure platforms and not over email or instant messaging.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Assuming rejected-application data is deleted immediately or that a deletion request has no effect on active applications.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe's careers site states a 30-day response window, withdrawal from active consideration, and legally required retention, so the assumption is factually wrong; this is process guidance, not an official screen.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Assuming Adobe uses a traditional annual rating or stack-ranking process; Adobe's published Check-in description says there is no formal rating or ranking.
anti_signals.risk_reason: A candidate who builds an answer around ratings, ranking, or annual review politics may be using a model Adobe says it replaced.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Treating Adobe as a single product or creative role when its career site separates engineering and product, design, research, sales, marketing, finance and operations, IT, customer experience, legal, and employee experience.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe's teams page describes distinct functions with different missions, so role fit should be argued at the function level.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Proposing an architecture or performance change without a measurement plan or before-and-after evidence.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe's engineering post is built around a measured startup bottleneck and a repeatable build-time method, so unmeasured optimization claims are weakly supported; this is a preparation signal, not an official disqualifier.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Treating a platform migration as a purely technical swap with no compatibility or developer-adoption plan.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe publicly commits to a compatibility window and a phased roadmap for its own extensibility migration, which implies migration planning is part of the work.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Treating an internship or graduate role as observation rather than mission-critical contribution.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe's early-career pages frame interns and graduates as contributors to products used at scale, so passive framing undersells the role's actual expectations.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Talking about values or creativity without commercial or customer evidence in go-to-market roles.
anti_signals.risk_reason: The Sales Academy explicitly pairs core-values demonstration with pipeline and revenue impact, so values language alone is incomplete for sales-track hiring.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Presenting design work as a solo achievement without acknowledging product, engineering, or research partners.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe Design managers say they listen for accurate credit-sharing and a clear view of the candidate's unique contribution; this is a preparation signal, not an official disqualifier.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Walking through final screens without explaining the problem, the audience, or the outcome.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe Design interviewers describe wanting the reason the work mattered and who it impacted before visual detail.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Treating a vulnerability as contained once a patch ticket is open, without describing the exposure window or compensating controls.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe's blog notes that patching takes time in practice and describes virtual patching and layered mitigations used during remediation windows. A ticket is not evidence that exposure was reduced.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Prioritizing remediation by severity score alone, without deployment context, internet reachability, or existing controls.
anti_signals.risk_reason: The blog says static severity scores do not always reflect real-world risk and that the same vulnerability can present different exposure depending on architecture and reachability.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Assuming unmanaged or forgotten infrastructure is low risk because no team has claimed it.
anti_signals.risk_reason: Adobe's blog names abandoned staging environments, decommissioned services with lingering credentials, and unmanaged infrastructure as exposure risks, and argues that organizations cannot protect assets they have not inventoried.

anti_signals.anti_signal: Treating third-party or open-source dependency risk as a procurement checkbox rather than a lifecycle control.
anti_signals.risk_reason: The blog describes dependency management, continuous monitoring, sandboxing, and malware analysis across the software lifecycle, and notes that upstream fixes may not be immediately available.

role_overlays.role_family: Research science and research engineering roles
signals: Combines academic discovery with applied work intended for product use.
Can explain the path from prototype or publication to a shipped feature.
Works with product engineers and designers rather than in isolation.

role_overlays.role_family: Product design and design engineering roles
signals: Shows a portfolio with explicit decisions, tradeoffs, and rejected alternatives.
Works across brand, product, content, visual, motion, or design engineering disciplines.
Collaborates with research, content strategy, product management, and engineering.
Credits collaborators accurately while making their own contribution unmistakable.
Explains why the work mattered to the people it served, not only how it looked.

role_overlays.role_family: Corporate and customer-facing functions at Adobe
signals: Maps experience to a specific function such as IT, finance and operations, customer experience, legal and government relations, or employee experience.
Explains that function's mission in Adobe's own terms rather than as generic back-office work.
Shows cross-functional collaboration with product, design, research, sales, or marketing.

role_overlays.role_family: Developer platform, SDK, and extensibility engineering
signals: Designs APIs and extension points with attention to compatibility, security, and long-term maintenance.
Balances internal architecture goals with external developer adoption and migration cost.
Uses performance measurement and build-system knowledge to improve the developer experience.

role_overlays.role_family: Interns, new graduates, and university programs
signals: Expects mission-critical contribution within a defined program window.
Brings a clear point of view and drive, including from non-technical backgrounds.
Uses structured training, mentorship, and certifications to accelerate.
Demonstrates Adobe's core values alongside measurable pipeline or revenue impact.
Shows coachability within a structured training program.
Builds customer-facing credibility early rather than waiting for a territory.

role_overlays.role_family: Design systems, platform design, and design program roles
signals: Balances system-level strategy with detailed requirements from multiple product teams.
Uses research, adoption, and usage data to prioritise roadmap work.
Plans migration, documentation, and support rather than a one-off release.

role_overlays.role_family: Security engineering, vulnerability management, and resilience
signals: Prioritizes by real exposure, reachability, and business context rather than severity alone.
Designs compensating controls for the window before a full fix is available.
Treats inventory, ownership, and monitoring as prerequisites for security.
Manages third-party and open-source risk across the software lifecycle.
Explains residual risk and what would change the decision.
